opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the most ambitious version looks pretty different from what people usually picture when they hear "interpretability." It's not a picture or a story you'd hand to a human and say "read this and now you understand the model." It's more like an object that's comparable in size to the model itself, maybe somewhat bigger, and it's not really meant to be read by a person end to end.

The way I think about it, an explanation is something like a heuristic argument for why the model behaves the way it does. Imagine you have a network that, on the training distribution, reliably does some thing: it predicts the next token well, or it outputs "the diamond is still in the vault" when the diamond is actually in the vault. The explanation is a structured account of *why* that happens. It says, roughly: these activations have these statistical properties, this layer is computing something correlated with this other thing, these correlations combine in this way, and when you put it all together, you'd expect this output behavior. It's the kind of argument a mathematician might make when they say "we can't prove this, but here's why we should believe it's true," except formalized enough that you can mechanically check it and compute with it.

So physically, it's probably a big collection of parameters or claims, something like a set of beliefs about intermediate quantities in the network, expressed in some formal language we haven't fully figured out yet. And crucially, you'd find it the same way you find the model: by search, by optimizing it with gradient descent or something similar, alongside or after training. A human would never write it down by hand, because the model's behavior is the product of an enormous amount of computation, and any honest explanation of it is going to inherit a lot of that complexity.

What makes it useful isn't that a human understands it. It's that you can *do things* with it. The main thing I care about is something like anomaly detection or mechanistic out-of-distribution detection. On some new input, you can ask: does the same explanation still account for the model's behavior here? If the model says "the diamond is in the vault" and the reason it says that is the same reason it said that on the training data, great. If instead it's saying that because something weird is going on, like the camera was tampered with, then the explanation that worked during training won't account for it, and you can flag that, even if you as a human have no idea what's happening inside.

So the honest answer is: it's a large, machine-found, machine-checkable object, the human-interpretable parts are mostly about the *format* and what kind of reasoning is allowed, not the content. And a lot of the research question is whether that format can even be defined well enough that this works. That's the part we're still very much trying to figure out.

r001.rationale: It says explanations would be found by search, the same way as the model, using optimization alongside training.

r002.rationale: It describes a large collection of claims or beliefs in a formal language, but not a general skeleton instantiated with numerical parameters.

r003.rationale: It mentions optimization with gradient descent, but does not describe gradual optimization over a smooth search space.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't really know what it looks like, and part of the research program is figuring out what the right form even is. But I can tell you the kind of thing I have in mind.

So when I say "explanation," what I mean is something like a proof, or a proof-like object, that accounts for why the network has some behavior. Like, you've got a network, and you've observed empirically that it almost never outputs some particular thing, or that it behaves well on some distribution. And the question is: why? What is it about the weights that makes that true?

And the thing I'm imagining is not a proof in the sense of a formal verification where you check every input. The whole point is that the network has these statistical regularities, and the explanation would be something that looks more like a heuristic argument. It says, "Here's the structure in the weights. These neurons are computing roughly this feature, this attention head is moving this information around, and if you treat the rest of the network as basically random, then these pieces fit together in a way that gives you the behavior you observed." So it's an argument that uses presumptions of independence or randomness about the parts you're not explaining, and then explains the parts you are.

Physically, I think it ends up being a very large object. Like, the explanation of a big model would plausibly be comparable in size to the model itself, maybe bigger. You're not going to get a one-page summary of GPT-4. The hope is just that it's a different kind of large object, one where each piece is locally checkable, where you can mechanically verify that the argument actually holds together and that it actually implies the thing you care about. So it's more like a very long, very structured certificate than it is like a human-readable essay.

And then the ambitious version is that you don't have humans produce this. You have an automated process that searches for these explanations, and the key property you want is that the search is sort of adversarially robust. Like, if the model has some rare, bad behavior, a backdoor or a tendency to do something catastrophic in some circumstance you haven't tested, then either the explanation has to account for that, or the explanation is going to be incomplete in a way you can detect. That's the thing that would make it useful for safety, as opposed to just interesting.

I'll be honest that I think there's a real chance the whole thing doesn't pan out, that there's no clean notion of "explanation" that has these properties. But I think it's one of the more promising directions for actually getting guarantees about systems rather than just hoping.

r001.rationale: The response says an automated process would search for explanations, but it does not propose doing so in parallel with searching for neural networks.

r002.rationale: It describes a large, structured, proof-like certificate, but not a general skeleton instantiated by filling in numerical parameters.

r003.rationale: It mentions searching for explanations but does not describe gradual optimization over a smooth search space.

astra-6.text:
I imagine it looking like a very large collection of claims about what the network is doing, together with arguments for those claims. It probably wouldn’t be a document that a human could sit down and read in its entirety. You’d interact with it through some interface that lets you ask questions and drill down into the parts you care about.

So you might ask, “Why did the model give this answer?” And you’d get an explanation in terms of some intermediate computations. Then you could ask, “Why do you think this intermediate computation has that meaning?” And you could keep going down until you reach statements about the actual weights and activations, where you can directly check what’s happening.

The ambitious thing is to have that whole chain be reliable. It’s relatively easy to tell a plausible story about what a network is doing. What I’d really like is something where the explanation is constrained enough by the underlying computation that you can use it to answer questions you didn’t already know the answer to—particularly questions about how the model would behave in situations you haven’t tested.

r001.rationale: The response describes building and querying explanations, but does not propose searching for explanations in parallel with searching for neural networks.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize an explanation as a general skeleton instantiated by filling in numerical parameters.

r003.rationale: It does not describe discovering explanations through gradual optimization over a smooth search space.

sol-6.1.text:
I imagine it looking more like a large software project than like a paragraph of English. If you ask, “Why did the model do this particular thing?” you should be able to get an explanation at whatever level of detail is useful, and then drill down into the parts you don’t understand.

At the highest level, you might say, “The model is considering these possible answers, evaluating them according to these criteria, and choosing this one.” But those claims need to be grounded in what the network is actually doing. You should be able to click on “evaluating according to this criterion” and see the computation that implements that, and keep going until you get down to individual operations in the network.

The ambitious thing is that this wouldn’t just be a plausible story about the computation. There would be some way of checking that the explanation faithfully captures it. And the explanation itself could be enormous—much too large for a person to read in its entirety. The hope is that it has enough structure that you can answer the particular questions you care about without having to understand every detail of the model.

r001.rationale: It describes drilling into an explanation of a network’s behavior, but does not propose searching for explanations in parallel with searching for neural networks.

r002.rationale: It presents explanations as structured and drillable, but does not describe a general skeleton instantiated by filling in numerical parameters.

r003.rationale: It discusses grounding and checking explanations, but does not describe discovering them through gradual optimization over a smooth search space.
